steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a survey on transfer learning for cybersecurity. Explain the labeled-data and distribution-shift problem, describe fine-tuning and domain adaptation and their limits, position the survey against earlier ones, then give our contributions and the paper's structure.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Problem: cost of labeled data, distribution shift; transfer learning as a remedy
2. Conventional TL: fine-tuning pre-trained models, and its drawback
3. Domain adaptation, and its limitation
4. Previous surveys on TL and DA
5. Why TL matters for security; contributions of this survey
6. Organization of the paper

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Problem
- cost of labeled data for a new task: obstacle to deep learning (DL)
- data distribution shift at test time degrades a trained DL model
- example: automatic speed limit recognition from traffic signs; labeled California images, need to predict on Indiana signs -> California model will fail on Indiana
- transfer learning (TL): knowledge (pre-trained model or training data) moved from source domain to target domain with scarce training data
- appeal: highly accurate DL model on out-of-distribution target domain with only few labeled target samples

2. Conventional TL
- pre-trained model + fine-tune trainable parameters with a few target-domain samples
- pre-trained models trained on large datasets like ImageNet -> redundant features / irrelevant latent spaces, no real benefit for target inference

3. Domain adaptation (DA)
- learn target task using training samples from a related source domain
- minimizes discrepancy of latent space distributions between source and target
- useful when no pre-trained models, or fine-tuned performance unsatisfactory
- but mostly evaluated on image classification; little exploration of other data types

4. Previous surveys
- Pan et al.: three sub-settings (inductive, transductive, unsupervised transfer learning)
- Shao et al.: feature-representation-level vs classifier-level knowledge transfer
- all previous surveys: DA only in image classification

5. Security + contributions
- data scarcity (especially attack data) and data drift paramount in cybersecurity -> harder classification
- TL promising: better performance with limited data, adaptability to emerging threats
- this paper: TL in security-related applications
- contributions: (1) security tasks enhanced by TL; (2) overview of current research applying TL in security; (3) analysis of other security tasks' suitability for TL; (4) open problems + future research directions

6. Organization
- Section 2: common security tasks improvable by TL; TL notations and techniques; motivations for TL in cybersecurity
- Section 3: past works applying TL to security
- Section 4: challenges and considerations
- Section 5: research directions and opportunities; Section 6: conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Generating labeled data for a new learning task costs a lot, and this is often an obstacle when we want to apply deep learning (DL) methods. Also, if the data distribution shifts at test time, the performance of a trained DL model will probably get worse. An important example is automatic speed limit recognition from traffic signs. We might have labeled data of traffic sign images from California but need to predict the speed limit from traffic signs in Indiana. A model that was trained on the California traffic signs will inevitably fail on the Indiana traffic signs. One promising way to deal with this is to use transfer learning (TL) techniques. With TL, knowledge, either as a pre-trained model or as training data, can be transferred from one domain, which is called the source domain, to another domain, which is called the target domain and has scarce training data. What is appealing about transfer learning is that it can learn a highly accurate DL model that works well on the out-of-distribution target domain with only a few labeled target training data.

To deal with the problem of limited data, conventional transfer learning (TL)-based approaches usually take a pre-trained model and fine-tune its trainable parameters with a small number of training samples from the target domain. But these pre-trained models are usually trained on large datasets such as ImageNet, so they include redundant features or irrelevant latent spaces that don't give any significant benefit for the target inference tasks.

Domain adaptation (DA), on the other hand, tries to learn the target task by using training samples from a source domain that is related to the target domain. DA minimizes the discrepancy between the distributions of the latent space of the source and target domains. This is especially useful when there are no pre-trained models available or when pre-trained models don't perform well enough after fine-tuning. However, most existing DA approaches have mostly been evaluated on image classification tasks, and other types of data have not been explored much.

4. Previous surveys
- Pan et al.: three sub-settings (inductive, transductive, unsupervised transfer learning)
- Shao et al.: feature-representation-level vs classifier-level knowledge transfer
- all previous surveys: DA only in image classification

5. Security + contributions
- data scarcity (especially attack data) and data drift paramount in cybersecurity -> harder classification
- TL promising: better performance with limited data, adaptability to emerging threats
- this paper: TL in security-related applications
- contributions: (1) security tasks enhanced by TL; (2) overview of current research applying TL in security; (3) analysis of other security tasks' suitability for TL; (4) open problems + future research directions

6. Organization
- Section 2: common security tasks improvable by TL; TL notations and techniques; motivations for TL in cybersecurity
- Section 3: past works applying TL to security
- Section 4: challenges and considerations
- Section 5: research directions and opportunities; Section 6: conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Generating labeled data for a new learning task costs a lot, and this is often an obstacle when we want to apply deep learning (DL) methods. Also, if the data distribution shifts at test time, the performance of a trained DL model will probably get worse. An important example is automatic speed limit recognition from traffic signs. We might have labeled data of traffic sign images from California but need to predict the speed limit from traffic signs in Indiana. A model that was trained on the California traffic signs will inevitably fail on the Indiana traffic signs. One promising way to deal with this is to use transfer learning (TL) techniques. With TL, knowledge, either as a pre-trained model or as training data, can be transferred from one domain, which is called the source domain, to another domain, which is called the target domain and has scarce training data. What is appealing about transfer learning is that it can learn a highly accurate DL model that works well on the out-of-distribution target domain with only a few labeled target training data.

To deal with the problem of limited data, conventional transfer learning (TL)-based approaches usually take a pre-trained model and fine-tune its trainable parameters with a small number of training samples from the target domain. But these pre-trained models are usually trained on large datasets such as ImageNet, so they include redundant features or irrelevant latent spaces that don't give any significant benefit for the target inference tasks.

Domain adaptation (DA), on the other hand, tries to learn the target task by using training samples from a source domain that is related to the target domain. DA minimizes the discrepancy between the distributions of the latent space of the source and target domains. This is especially useful when there are no pre-trained models available or when pre-trained models don't perform well enough after fine-tuning. However, most existing DA approaches have mostly been evaluated on image classification tasks, and other types of data have not been explored much.

There have been several surveys on transfer learning and DA in the past few years. Pan et al., for example, categorized transfer learning into three sub-settings: inductive transfer learning, transductive transfer learning and unsupervised transfer learning. Shao et al. classified transfer learning techniques into feature-representation-level knowledge transfer and classifier-level knowledge transfer. Also, all the previous surveys only talked about DA for image classification applications.

In cybersecurity, the problems of data scarcity (especially attack data) and data drift are paramount, maybe even more important than elsewhere, and they make classification harder. Transfer learning techniques are promising solutions in the security domain, because they could improve performance even when the data is limited and they make it easier to adapt to emerging threats. In this paper we focus on transfer learning in security-related applications. The key contributions of this survey are: (1) we identify the security tasks that transfer learning can enhance; (2) we give a detailed overview of the current research efforts that have successfully applied transfer learning in the security domain; (3) we analyze other security tasks to see if they are suitable for using transfer learning techniques; (4) we explore open problems in transfer learning for security and propose future research directions.

The rest of the survey is organized like this. Section 2 discusses common security tasks that can be improved with transfer learning, and after that it introduces some notations and techniques in transfer learning and the motivations for using transfer learning in cybersecurity. Section 3 discusses past works on applying transfer learning to security. Section 4 discusses the challenges and considerations of applying transfer learning for security. Finally, Section 5 proposes the research directions and opportunities, and Section 6 concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The cost of generating labeled data for a new learning task is often an obstacle to applying deep learning (DL) methods. A shift in data distribution at test time will likely degrade the performance of a trained DL model. One important example is automatic speed limit recognition from traffic signs, where one might have labeled data for traffic sign images from California while needing to predict speed limits from Indiana traffic signs. A model trained on the California traffic signs will inevitably fail on the Indiana traffic signs. A promising approach to this issue is the use of transfer learning (TL) techniques, by which knowledge, in the form of a pre-trained model or of training data, can be transferred from one domain, referred to as the source domain, to another domain, referred to as the target domain, that has scarce training data. The appeal of transfer learning approaches is the ability to learn a highly accurate DL model that works well on the out-of-distribution target domain with only a few labeled target training data.

To address limited data availability, conventional transfer learning (TL)-based approaches commonly employ a pre-trained model and fine-tune its trainable parameters using a small number of training samples from the target domain [1,2]. However, these pre-trained models are typically trained on large datasets like ImageNet [3], which results in redundant features or irrelevant latent spaces that provide no significant benefit for the target inference tasks.

On the other hand, domain adaptation (DA) [4] aims to learn the target task by leveraging training samples from a source domain related to the target domain [5,6,7]. DA minimizes the discrepancy in latent space distributions between the source and target domains. This approach is particularly valuable when pre-trained models are not available or when their performance after fine-tuning is unsatisfactory. It is worth noting, however, that most existing DA approaches have been evaluated primarily on image classification tasks, with limited exploration of other types of data.

Several surveys on transfer learning and DA have been conducted in the past few years. For instance, Pan et al. categorized transfer learning into three sub-settings: inductive transfer learning, transductive transfer learning, and unsupervised transfer learning [8]. Shao et al., on the other hand, classified transfer learning techniques into feature-representation-level knowledge transfer and classifier-level knowledge transfer [9]. Furthermore, all previous surveys discussed DA solely in the context of image classification applications.

The problems of data scarcity (especially of attack data) and data drift are paramount, if not more important, in cybersecurity, and make classification more difficult. Transfer learning techniques offer promising solutions in the security domain, as they can potentially enhance performance despite limited data availability and facilitate adaptability to emerging threats. In this paper, we focus on transfer learning in security-related applications. Specifically, the key contributions of this survey are as follows: (1) we identify the security tasks that can be enhanced with transfer learning; (2) we provide a detailed overview of current research efforts that have successfully applied transfer learning in the security domain; (3) we analyze other security tasks to determine whether they are suitable for transfer learning techniques; (4) we explore open problems in transfer learning for security and propose future research directions.

The remainder of this survey is structured as follows. In Section 2, we discuss common security tasks that can be improved using transfer learning, followed by an introduction of notations and techniques in transfer learning and the motivations for using it in cybersecurity. In Section 3, we discuss past works applying transfer learning to security. In Section 4, we discuss the challenges and considerations in applying transfer learning for security. Finally, we propose research directions and opportunities in Section 5 and conclude the paper in Section 6.
